expect.statement: In bodies examined after death, the measured concentration of a drug in blood can differ from the concentration at the moment of death, and from one blood vessel to another in the same body, by amounts that vary between drugs and between bodies and that cannot be predicted for a given death. In four suspected overdose deaths chosen by forensic medicine authors in Dundee and Edmonton to illustrate the problem (tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and the sleeping medicine flurazepam; autopsy about 7 to 48 hours after death; office and period not stated), blood drawn separately from up to 11 vessels of the same body differed 3.5- to 6.6-fold for each drug (editors' calculation from the printed ranges), usually highest in central vessels near the lungs and liver and lowest in the subclavian or femoral veins, though in one case the lowest value was in the pulmonary artery; in the only person with a blood sample from life, taken in hospital about 1 to 2 hours before death, every post-mortem sample, femoral blood included, held 1.8 to 7.9 times as much imipramine (editors' calculation). The authors attribute the differences to drug diffusing out of organs after death, but no body was sampled more than once and unabsorbed drug was still in the gut in three of the four, so part of the differences may have arisen before death (Pounder & Jones, 1990). A compilation of 10,993 results from 5,375 post-mortem cases for 50 compounds (published reports found by keyword searching, plus a Finnish national laboratory database for 2000 to 2018; cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids were left out) found, where the same case had both values, median ratios to femoral blood across drugs of 1.27 for other blood such as heart blood (576 results), 0.99 for muscle, 0.45 for the fluid of the eye (vitreous humour), 1.84 for brain, 2.03 for heart muscle, 5.06 for liver and 5.52 for bile, with tenfold or larger differences between drugs for most specimens (for other blood, morphine 1.26 and methamphetamine 1.50); no range or interval is given for any ratio, and cause of death and time since death could not be taken into account (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019). A review of 87 studies selected from a two-database search in April 2025 reports that in animal experiments drug levels in heart blood rose within minutes of death; that in human bodies sampled more than once, femoral blood, the sample thought least open to change (Ferner, 2008), rose significantly after death for about a dozen drugs, among them fentanyl and methadone, and fell for others, among them 6-MAM (the marker of heroin) and THC; and that the first sample in these human studies was taken on average about 17 hours after death (range 1 to 292 hours), so earlier change was not seen. It gives no sizes, does not appraise the studies, judges that a heart-to-femoral blood ratio shows that change after death occurred but not how much, and concludes that the size of the change cannot yet be tied to drug properties or to features of the case (Borra et al., 2026). A 2003 practitioners' review lists single approximate heart-to-peripheral blood ratios for about 100 drugs without case numbers or sources (for example morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3), higher than the compilation's paired medians for several of the same drugs (Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ketola & Kriikku, 2019), and a clinical pharmacologist's review adds that post-mortem whole blood is compared with plasma or serum values from living patients, and that the ratio between the two differs by drug even in life (Ferner, 2008). Change can run both ways: a level after death can be higher than in life, which can make a drug look more involved in a death than it was, or lower, for drugs that break down or are lost after death. The evidence consists of selected case series, an unappraised compilation dominated by published poisoning cases, and narrative reviews, mostly about medicines; how often, and by how much, a level changes in an ordinary death is not known. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

set.plain: Can the amount of a drug in the blood change after death? Yes. In four selected overdose deaths, levels in different blood vessels differed about 3 to 7 times for the drugs taken in overdose; a medicine given in hospital varied less. In one person tested in hospital before death, all later imipramine samples were about 2 to 8 times higher. A compilation found large differences between drugs and specimens. Its typical other-blood ratio was about a quarter above thigh blood, but that was a median across drug-specific medians, not an average of all deaths. Repeated tests after death found rises for some drugs and falls for others. The size and frequency of these changes in ordinary deaths remain unknown.
set.magnitude: Within one body (four selected overdoses, autopsy about 7 to 48 h after death): highest to lowest blood value 3.5- to 6.6-fold per drug taken in the overdose (editors' calculation; doxepin 3.5, amobarbital 6.0, secobarbital 6.5, pentobarbital 6.2, clomipramine 5.4, flurazepam 6.6, imipramine 4.4; lidocaine given in hospital 1.6). One case with a sample from life: post-mortem imipramine 4.1–18.1 mg/L against 2.3 mg/L in hospital, 1.8- to 7.9-fold. Medians across drug-specific medians of paired within-case ratios (printed number of results): other blood 1.27 (576), muscle 0.99 (385), vitreous humour 0.45 (356), brain 1.84 (565), heart 2.03 (185), kidney 2.86 (401), lung 3.69 (187), spleen 4.25 (71), liver 5.06 (1,697), bile 5.52 (537); between drugs, liver 0.95–54.29, vitreous 0.03–1.59, other blood 0.90–14.61; other blood for morphine 1.26 (53), methamphetamine 1.50 (9). Human repeated sampling: first sample on average 17 h after death (range 1–292 h) where reported or estimated; rises in femoral blood for about 12 drugs, falls for 5 (no sizes). Narrative-review approximate heart-to-peripheral values without case counts or per-value sources (82 numeric-labelled entries among 98 distinct labels, including a nicotine/cotinine annotation; two ranges): morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5–2.3; more than 10% above the compilation's paired other-blood median for 17 of 24 drugs in both (editors' comparison). No within-drug intervals are given. The Table 3 N columns sum to 4,960 but include one oxazepam brain count without a printed ratio; the counts are results, not distinct deaths.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: The site differences come from four overdose deaths chosen to illustrate the problem, with no denominator and no serial sampling (card sc_pounder_1990, JBI high); the ratios come from a compilation drawn mostly from published reports, some of them focused on poisonings, without study-level appraisal or uncertainty estimates (its number-weighted descriptive summaries do not supply study-level precision weighting or within-drug spread) (card sc_ketola_2019, AMSTAR 2 by analogy, critically low); the changes over time are relayed without sizes from a review that does not appraise its studies (card sc_borra_2026). Selection of striking cases could make the differences look larger than in ordinary deaths.

set.plain: Can a blood test after death show that a drug caused the death? Not on its own. In an English autopsy study, MDMA levels in deaths put down to MDMA overlapped with levels in people who died of injuries. A review reports similar findings for morphine in an older US study. Finnish data compare levels after death with treatment reference ranges, rather than testing living patients in the same study. At one US centre, full autopsy and toxicology led to a different final classification in both directions: some suspected drug deaths were judged unrelated to drugs, and some unsuspected deaths were judged drug-related. That study examined drug presence, not blood levels. The certifiers' knowledge and rules limit what these comparisons can show.

expect.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether cannabis use causes sudden deaths from heart or blood-vessel problems, and in the one large autopsy registry read here no death was certified as a poisoning by THC, the main active substance of cannabis. A 2019 narrative review by three forensic medicine authors in Victoria, Australia (English-language reports found in two databases, with no stated selection rules or appraisal) counted six publications describing 13 deaths, all of men aged 17 to 52, that the case authors, and in one case a coroner, linked to recent cannabis use: 8 of the 13 had significant coronary artery disease or other pathology, THC was measured in blood in 8 (1.9 to 22 ng/mL), the other 5 rested on urine tests or the person's history (in one of them no THC was found in blood, yet the coroner found cannabis a secondary cause), alcohol was found in 2, two died days after reaching hospital and one had no autopsy (Drummer et al., 2019). The reviewers write that the larger studies and systematic reviews leave the link between cannabis use and death from heart disease unclear and the risk probably rare, that no minimum blood THC level can show cause because of delays between death and sampling (most laboratories detect 1 to 2 ng/mL, and lower values may reflect use days earlier), and that a blood THC test, not urine or history alone, is needed to link a death to recent use; yet they recommend that, with very recent use, a positive blood THC and a possible heart or brain-vessel cause, cannabis be considered at least a contributory cause of a sudden death, that THC be recorded in death statistics, and they call the 13 deaths 'very likely to be an under-estimate of the true incidence', without data on how many deaths are missed (Drummer et al., 2019). The review also notes, without details or numbers, that some deaths have been attributed to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (severe repeated vomiting; four references, not read here; Drummer et al., 2019). set.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether cannabis use causes sudden deaths from heart or blood-vessel problems, and the Finnish autopsy table cited here reports 0%, rounded to whole percent, as fatal poisonings with THC (the main active substance of cannabis) as the main finding. This is not an exact count of zero, does not cover every possible contribution, and is not a worldwide mortality rate. A 2019 narrative review by three forensic medicine authors in Victoria, Australia (English-language reports found in two databases, with broad inclusion rules but no search dates, screening counts or study-level appraisal) counted six publications describing 13 deaths, all of men aged 17 to 52, that the case authors, and in one case a coroner, linked to recent cannabis use: 8 of the 13 had significant coronary artery disease or other pathology, THC was measured in blood in 8 (1.9 to 22 ng/mL), the other 5 rested on urine tests or the person's history (in one of them no THC was found in blood, yet the coroner found cannabis a secondary cause), alcohol was found in 2, two died days after reaching hospital and one had no autopsy (Drummer et al., 2019). The reviewers write that the larger studies and systematic reviews leave the link between cannabis use and death from heart disease unclear and the risk probably rare, that it may not be possible to give a minimum causal blood THC level because of delays between death and sampling (most laboratories detect 1 to 2 ng/mL, and lower values may reflect use days earlier), and that a blood THC test, not urine or history alone, is needed to link a death to recent use; yet they recommend that, with very recent use, a positive blood THC and a possible heart or brain-vessel cause, cannabis be considered at least a contributory cause of a sudden death, that THC be recorded in death statistics, and they call the 13 deaths 'very likely to be an under-estimate of the true incidence', without data on how many deaths are missed (Drummer et al., 2019). The review also notes, without details or numbers, that some deaths have been attributed to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (severe repeated vomiting; four references, not read here; Drummer et al., 2019). They relay, second-hand, studies pointing both ways: a heart-attack risk 4.8 times the baseline (95% CI 2.9 to 9.5) in the first hour after smoking cannabis, as the review relays it (the primary interval was not checked), in a case-crossover study of 3,882 people, and a higher death rate after a heart attack with weekly use (hazard ratio 4.2, 1.2 to 14, in 1,913 people), against no association with cardiovascular death in 5,113 young US adults followed for more than 25 years and no increase in overall in-hospital mortality in more than two million US heart-attack admissions, and two systematic reviews that disagree; the review's statement that eleven of its twelve tabulated studies showed raised risk is not borne out by its own table (Drummer et al., 2019). In Finland, among 57,903 medico-legal autopsies with full drug testing in 2000 to 2010, THC was found in femoral blood in 347 deaths (median 0.002 mg/L, that is 2 ng/mL), and the table prints 0% certified as fatal poisonings with THC as the main finding. One of 347 would also round to 0% under ordinary rounding, so the exact count is not established by that percentage alone (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014). THC levels after death are hard to read: THC in femoral blood fell between repeated samples after death in one study, while other before/after comparisons reported higher THC after death than in samples from life; the comparisons have different timing and possible matrix differences and do not isolate redistribution from every other process (Borra et al., 2026, second-hand, without effect sizes), and a review gives a factor of 1.6 for calculating plasma cannabinoid concentrations from whole blood, without validating it for every post-mortem THC case (Leikin & Watson, 2003, second-hand). The case reports have no comparison group and cannot show how often THC is present in sudden deaths that cannabis did not cause, so these reports cannot validate the reviewers' attribution rule or an undercount estimate. Their criteria include excluding other reasonable explanations and considering a plausible mechanism as well as THC and the circumstances. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
set.plain: Can cannabis cause a sudden death? The evidence read here does not settle this. A review collected 13 deaths linked to recent use, all in men; 8 had significant heart disease or other illness, alcohol was found in 2, and 5 lacked a blood THC result showing recent use. Some died days after hospital admission. The reports have no comparison group. Larger studies, known here through the review, point both ways for heart attacks and death; some found no increased mortality. The Finnish table prints 0% as poisonings mainly attributed to THC, rounded to whole percent; it does not give an exact zero count or settle other forms of contribution. The reviewers encourage counting cannabis as a contributor in appropriate cases but give no estimate of missed deaths. Certainty remains very low.
set.magnitude: Not estimable as a risk. Case reports (Drummer et al., 2019): 13 deaths, men aged 17–52 (median 37); coronary disease or other pathology 8/13; blood THC measured in 8 (1.9–22 ng/mL), urine or history only in 5 (one blood-negative); alcohol in 2 (0.04% and 0.119%). Relayed: acute myocardial infarction 4.8 (95% CI 2.9–9.5) in the first hour after smoking, as relayed (primary interval unread); 1.7 (0.6–5.1) in the second hour in the text, labelled within 2 h in Table 3 (case-crossover, n = 3,882); mortality after MI, HR 4.2 (1.2–14) weekly use, 2.5 (0.9–7.3) less than weekly (n = 1,913); CARDIA (n = 5,113, over 25 years): no association with cardiovascular mortality. Desai summary: no increase in overall mortality in over two million AMI admissions, despite a separate AMI association. Finland 2000–2010: THC in femoral blood in 347 deaths, median 0.002 mg/L, 97.5th percentile 0.024 mg/L, 0% certified as fatal poisoning with THC as the main finding, rounded to whole percent; no exact zero count established. These Finnish values are inherited checked anchors, not freshly verified against the unavailable primary by reader 405.

debate.question: Can using cannabis cause a sudden death, for example by setting off a heart attack or a dangerous heart rhythm, and should such deaths be counted as cannabis deaths?
debate.evidence_yes: Case reports describe 13 men aged 17 to 52 whose deaths the case authors or a coroner linked to recent cannabis use, 8 of them with THC measured in blood (1.9 to 22 ng/mL) and five described as having little obvious heart disease; in one case a coroner found cannabis a secondary cause of death (Drummer et al., 2019). The same review describes 35 people in 31 case reports who reached hospital with cardiovascular episodes, most involving chest pain, rhythm problems or coronary clots (18 heart attacks were confirmed by blood tests; the text gives 5 strokes or transient attacks while Table 1 contains 6) during or soon after cannabis use, 24 of them without evidence of coronary artery disease (Drummer et al., 2019). As relayed, a case-crossover study of 3,882 people with a heart attack is relayed as finding a risk 4.8 times the baseline (95% CI 2.9 to 9.5; primary interval not read) in the hour after smoking cannabis; among 1,913 people after a heart attack the death rate was higher with weekly use (hazard ratio 4.2, 1.2 to 14); in national hospital data ischaemic stroke was more common (adjusted risk ratio 1.17, 1.15 to 1.20); among 2,097 people with a heart attack before age 51, cardiovascular death was more common (adjusted hazard ratio 2.22, printed as a 90% CI of 1.27 to 3.70); and a systematic review of 81 case reports and 29 observational studies found an association with cardiovascular disease, stronger for ischaemic stroke (Drummer et al., 2019). The review also notes, without numbers, deaths attributed to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (Drummer et al., 2019). The forensic reviewers hold that a small number of susceptible people with other illnesses could be harmed, and that when use was very recent, blood THC is positive and the death could be cardiac or cerebrovascular, cannabis should be recorded as at least a contributory cause so that its harm is not underestimated (Drummer et al., 2019).
debate.evidence_no: In the Finnish autopsy registry, the table for 347 deaths with THC in femoral blood in 2000 to 2010 gives 0% as fatal poisonings with THC as the main finding, rounded to whole percent; this does not establish exactly zero or absence of any contribution (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014). Of the 13 published deaths, 8 had significant coronary disease or other pathology, alcohol was found in 2 (blood alcohol 0.04% and 0.119%), 5 lacked the blood THC result that the reviewers themselves require to link a death to recent use, one had no THC in blood, two died days after reaching hospital and one had no autopsy (Drummer et al., 2019). The reviewers state that the link with death from heart disease is not clear, that the events described may have other causes such as undiagnosed rhythm disorders or tobacco smoking, and that the risk is probably rare (Drummer et al., 2019). As relayed, the CARDIA cohort of 5,113 young US adults followed for 25 years found no association of cannabis use with cardiovascular death; a cohort of 3,886 people followed for 18 years found 29% higher mortality with cannabis use that was not statistically significant; and a systematic review found no compelling evidence linking cannabis use with death, including from heart attack (Drummer et al., 2019). The review's count of eleven of twelve studies showing raised risk is not borne out by its own table, in which at most 8 rows report a raised estimate, some not significant (first reader's reading of Drummer et al., 2019). The review also relays no increase in overall in-hospital mortality in more than two million US heart-attack admissions (Desai), although an AMI association is reported separately. The primary epidemiological papers were not read here.
debate.neither_can_show: Case reports are published because someone suspected a link; deaths with THC present that were judged unrelated go unpublished, so the reports cannot show how often a link is real or how often THC is found in sudden deaths in general, and they have no comparison group. THC in blood after death does not show when cannabis was used or how much: the reviewers give no validated minimum level and say a causal minimum may not be possible to provide, laboratories detect down to 1 to 2 ng/mL, low values may reflect use days earlier, THC levels change after death, and whole blood differs from the serum used for living values (Drummer et al., 2019; Borra et al., 2026; Leikin & Watson, 2003). Certification in the registry rests on pathologists' judgment without stated criteria, so a death set off by cannabis could be put down to heart disease, and a death in which cannabis was only present could be put down to cannabis. The epidemiological studies rely mostly on self-reported use or hospital coding, are known here only second-hand, and measure heart attacks and strokes more often than deaths. The Finnish percentage addresses poisoning with THC as the main finding, not every possible causal contribution. Borra relays both falling THC between post-mortem samples and higher post-mortem than ante-mortem THC; these are different comparisons with additional timing and matrix limits. The 1.6 cannabinoid matrix factor is second-hand advice, not validated for every individual death.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). The selected reports cannot determine whether cannabis triggered a death or estimate how often it does. They include significant pathology, possible other explanations, delayed deaths and missing blood THC confirmation. The Finnish table's rounded 0% for fatal poisoning with THC as the main finding does not establish an exact zero count or rule out other contribution. Epidemiology is relayed second-hand, concerns heart attacks or strokes more often than mortality, and includes positive and null findings. The reviewers encourage attribution in appropriate cases and believe deaths are undercounted, but provide no undercount estimate or validation of the attribution criteria. Those criteria include competing explanations and a plausible mechanism as well as the test result and circumstances.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A population-based study of sudden cardiac deaths with complete toxicology (blood THC with the time from death to sampling recorded), compared with suitable controls such as deaths from external causes or living people from the same population, with coronary disease, tobacco and alcohol measured, to estimate whether recent cannabis use raises the risk of sudden cardiac death and how often THC is present in such deaths without having contributed; and agreement studies of certification rules for drug contribution, tested on pathologists who do not know the toxicology results.
